html:
The civil code of the Ottoman Empire, issued in parts between 1869 and 1876. It was the first time a Muslim state set out the rules of Islamic law in the form of a modern code.

During the Tanzimat reforms, some officials wanted to copy the French civil code, the Napoleonic Code. A committee led by the scholar and statesman Ahmed Cevdet Pasha chose another way. They took the rules of contract, sale, rent, debt, partnership and evidence from the Hanafi school of sharia, the official school of the empire, and set them out in 1,851 numbered articles. Judges no longer had to dig through centuries of legal writing in Arabic to find the rule.

Family law and inheritance were left out. They stayed with the religious courts.

The Mecelle outlived the empire. Turkey replaced it in 1926 when it adopted the Swiss civil code. In other former Ottoman lands, from Iraq to Jordan and Palestine, it stayed in force for decades; Israel repealed its last parts only in 1984.
sum: The civil code of the Ottoman Empire, issued in parts between 1869 and 1876. It was the first time a Muslim state set out the rules of Islamic law in the form of a modern code.
